title: What Is a GMP Contract? Scope Risk Every GC Estimator Needs to Know
summary: GMP contracts cap your cost but not your scope exposure. Learn what GCs miss at bid and how to protect margin before the GMP is set.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- A GMP (Guaranteed Maximum Price) contract caps what the owner pays. It does not cap what you spend.
- Scope gaps set during pre-construction become your liability, not change orders, once the GMP is signed.
- The riskiest moment in a GMP project is not construction. It is the period between the design documents and the signed GMP.
- The same habits that protect lump sum margin protect GMP margin. The penalty for skipping them is higher.
- Tools like[Provision's Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) exist specifically to surface scope gaps and contract exposure before that number is locked.


## What Is a GMP Contract in Construction?


A Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) contract sets a ceiling on what the owner pays for a project. If costs exceed that ceiling, the general contractor absorbs the difference. If costs come in under it, savings are typically shared between the owner and GC under a predetermined split.


GMP contracts are most common in Construction Manager at Risk (CM at Risk) and design-build delivery. They give owners cost certainty before construction starts. They give GCs a margin opportunity if the project is well-run. They punish estimating errors more than almost any other contract type.


The cap sounds straightforward. The exposure is not.


## GMP vs. Lump Sum: What Changes for the Estimator


Both contract types require a fixed price. The difference is what that price is based on when you sign it.


Factor Lump Sum GMP


Design at time of pricing Typically complete (100% CDs) Often incomplete (60–80% DDs or schematic)


Scope definition Owner's drawings and specs define scope GC must define scope from incomplete documents


Change order mechanism Owner changes trigger COs Design evolution within GMP is often the GC's risk


Contingency GC carries contingency internally Explicit GMP contingency line, negotiated with owner


Scope gap liability Can sometimes argue omission against owner's documents Harder to argue: GC often accepted scope responsibility at GMP


On a lump sum, the owner's drawings define what you price. If they're incomplete or wrong, you have an argument. On a GMP signed against 60% design development drawings, you accepted responsibility for a scope that did not fully exist yet. That is the exposure.


## Why GMP Scope Risk Is Different


On a standard lump sum bid, your scope risk is real but bounded. If a spec section is missing, you can point to the document set. The owner owns the incomplete design.


On a GMP project, the GC often gets involved earlier, when design is still incomplete. That early involvement is the value proposition for the owner. It is also how scope exposure transfers to the GC.


Three things make GMP scope risk distinct:


### 1. You are pricing design intent, not complete drawings


At the GMP stage, you may be working from 60% design development or even schematic drawings. Every assumption you embed in that number becomes your problem if the final drawings say something different.


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it plainly: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." That quote comes from Provision's research with 200+ general contractors, documented in the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) . It describes subcontractor behavior, but it applies equally to the owner when a GC misses scope in a GMP.


### 2. Readily inferable language cuts both ways


Standard contract language often requires the GC to include work that is "reasonably inferable" from the documents, even if not explicitly shown. On a GMP signed against incomplete drawings, the question of what was inferable at the time of signing becomes a dispute.


Arcadis tracked the average North American construction dispute value at $60.1 million in its 2024 Global Construction Disputes Report. Errors and omissions in contract documents rank among the top causes of those disputes in North America. GMP projects are not immune. They are more exposed, because the GC accepted scope risk earlier in the design process.


A Senior PM at a Canadian ICI GC described the pressure: "Our construction management clients expect us to find the scope gaps in the design too now. They expect us to be designers and engineers." That expectation lands on the estimator's desk at GMP time.


### 3. Design evolution during construction is the GC's problem


Once the GMP is signed, the owner expects the design to stay within that number. If the architect adds detail during construction document development, and that detail was arguably within the original design intent, the owner will argue it was already in the GMP. The GC often has no clean argument that it was not.


This is not theoretical. A $300,000 lead-lined glass scope gap on a hospital imaging suite, documented in the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , illustrates exactly this pattern. The GC absorbed the cost under "readily inferable" language because the imaging suite was in the program from day one. The spec requirement was not in the drawings at GMP time. It was in the final CDs.


## Where GCs Miss Scope Before the GMP Is Set


Most GMP scope gaps do not come from careless estimating. They come from structural problems in how pre-construction teams review incomplete documents.


### The document set is reviewed one file at a time


An estimator reviews the architectural drawings. A different estimator reviews the structural drawings. Nobody cross-references them against each other. The $45,000 stone-depth mismatch between civil, structural, and architectural drawings on a single slab (another documented case from the Scope Gap Playbook) is exactly this kind of gap. Each drawing was reviewed. The conflict between them was not.


### Addenda updates do not reach every scope package


Between the GMP estimate and the buyout of subcontractors, the design evolves. Addenda land. Specifications change. If your scope packages were written against the original document set, your subs are pricing an earlier version of the project. The GC owns the gap between what the subs priced and what the final documents require.


### Trade coordination gaps are priced by nobody


Provision's Scope Gap Index analyzed 1,290 scope packages across 24 projects from 16 general contractors in Q3 2026. It found that 74% of packages had at least one coordination flag: a model-generated flag marking work that appears to sit between two trades, which an estimator still needs to review and confirm.


In a GMP context, any item confirmed as unassigned is the GC's problem. The owner's GMP does not expand to cover them. See the full breakdown at the[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) .


### The scope sheet is not specific enough


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described the standard for scope specificity this way: "It's descriptive: bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"


On a GMP project, vague scope packages create two problems: subs undercut their number at buyout, and the GC has no documented basis for what was included at GMP time.


## The Eight Habits That Protect GMP Margin


Provision's research with 200+ GCs produced eight habits shared by the firms with the best pre-construction margins. All eight apply on GMP projects. Three are especially critical:


### Habit 1: Drawings-first, not boilerplate-first


Start scope packages from the actual drawing set for this project. Do not start from a template written for a similar job. GMP documents at 60% design are not interchangeable with 100% CDs from a previous project. Boilerplate scope written for complete drawings will miss what is not yet drawn.


### Habit 2: Front-load the buyout conversations


The gap between the GMP estimate and actual subcontractor buyout is where margin lives or dies. If the GMP assumed $800,000 for mechanical work and buyout comes in at $950,000, somebody absorbs $150,000. Talking to key subs before the GMP is set narrows that gap. It does not eliminate it, but it gives the estimator a real number to anchor against.


A Director of Pre-Construction at a Mid-Market Southeast GC described the challenge: "Pre-con is working in the scope sheet world and project management is working in the scopes of work." The handoff between those two worlds is where GMP margin erodes.


### Habit 3: The pre-issue scope review checkpoint


Before scope packages go to subs, run one review of the full document set together. Not one file at a time. Not one estimator's section at a time. The full set, looking for conflicts between what different trades have been told and what the drawings actually show. This is the step most GCs skip when time is short. It is the step that catches the $400,000 missed roof cover board on a $50 million project, documented in the Scope Gap Playbook.


For a deeper look at all eight habits and the anti-patterns that undercut them, read the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from 200+ GC interviews.


## The Anti-Patterns That Hurt GMP Estimates the Most


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) documents the habits that consistently produce scope gaps. On GMP projects, three are especially damaging:


- **"As per plans and specs."** This is the most-cited anti-pattern in the playbook. It is also the riskiest phrase in a GMP scope package, because "plans and specs" at GMP time is an incomplete document set. If your scope says "as per plans and specs" and the final CDs add scope, you have no written basis for a change order.
- **Copy-paste from the previous similar job.** GMP projects are priced against a specific design intent at a specific point in time. A scope package written for a previous hospital does not capture the design evolution of this hospital at this stage.
- **The five-minutes-before-bid review.** On a GMP, there is no bid day in the traditional sense. There is a GMP proposal date, often after weeks of pre-construction collaboration. The pace creates a false sense of comfort. Teams assume issues were caught during pre-construction meetings. They were not all caught.

## What to Do Before You Sign a GMP


A GMP project rewards the GC who does the most thorough pre-construction work. Here is a practical checklist for the period between design engagement and GMP execution:


1. **Map the document set at the time of GMP pricing.** Document exactly which drawings, specifications, and addenda the GMP is based on. This is your baseline for every future scope discussion.
2. **Run a full cross-document review.** Look for conflicts between disciplines. Structural versus architectural. MEP versus architectural. Civil versus structural. These conflicts produce unassigned scope.
3. **Build trade-specific scope packages from these documents.** Do not issue generic bid invitations. Write scope packages that name exactly what each trade is and is not responsible for, with citations back to the GMP document set.
4. **Get real sub numbers on key trades before signing.** For the top four or five trades by value, run scope packages by key subs before the GMP is locked. Use their feedback to validate your assumptions.
5. **Define the GMP contingency allocation clearly.** Document what your contingency covers and what it does not. Scope gaps discovered after GMP signing are not the same as design changes. Your contingency strategy should treat them differently.
6. **Review the contract language on design evolution.** Understand exactly when design development triggers an owner change versus when it falls within the original GMP scope. Negotiate the definition of "readily inferable" before you sign.
7. **Build a document log for addenda management.** As the design evolves post-GMP, every addendum needs to be evaluated against the GMP scope baseline. This is not an optional step. It is how you build the paper trail for legitimate change orders.


For a deeper look at trade-specific scope gaps that surface repeatedly on GMP projects, see[Chapter 5 of the Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) , which covers MEP, envelope, concrete, and specialty trade gaps drawn from 200+ GC interviews.


## The Bottom Line on GMP Scope Risk


A GMP contract gives your owner cost certainty. It gives you an obligation to deliver a scope that is not yet fully defined when you sign it. The margin opportunity in a GMP project is real. So is the downside when scope gaps surface during construction, after the number is locked.


The firms that consistently protect GMP margin are not smarter than their competitors. They are more systematic. They build complete scope packages earlier. They cross-reference the full document set. They get real sub feedback before the GMP is set. And they document every assumption so they can defend it later.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What does GMP mean in a construction contract?


GMP stands for Guaranteed Maximum Price. The GC agrees to complete the project for no more than the GMP amount. If final costs exceed it, the GC absorbs the difference. If costs come in under it, savings are typically shared between the owner and GC under a predetermined split.


### How is a GMP contract different from a lump sum contract?


Both set a fixed price, but lump sum contracts are typically priced against 100% complete construction documents. GMP contracts are often priced against incomplete design development drawings. That means the GC accepts scope responsibility for work that is not yet fully defined, which creates higher scope risk than a standard lump sum bid.


### What is the biggest scope risk in a GMP project?


The biggest risk is pricing design intent instead of complete drawings. When the GMP is set against 60–80% design documents, every assumption embedded in the estimate becomes the GC's problem if the final CDs show something different. Scope gaps discovered after the GMP is signed are rarely recoverable as owner change orders.


### What does "readily inferable" mean in a GMP contract?


Readily inferable language requires the GC to include work that a reasonable contractor would have understood to be part of the project, even if it was not explicitly shown in the documents at GMP time. On incomplete design documents, this language transfers significant scope risk to the GC. Negotiating its definition before signing is essential.


### How should a GC manage scope during GMP buyout?


Issue trade-specific scope packages that cite the exact drawings and specifications from the GMP document set. Get real sub numbers on major trades before the GMP is finalized. Document every scope inclusion and exclusion. As addenda arrive post-GMP, evaluate each one against the original scope baseline and issue revised packages where needed.


### Can AI tools help with GMP scope review?


Yes. Provision's Scope Agent reads the full digital document set, including drawings and specs together, and generates trade-specific scope packages with every item source-traced to the exact page. It reaches 97.01% match accuracy on scope item extraction. Risk Review flags contract exposures and "readily inferable" language with 99% accuracy on risk identification, cited to the exact clause.


### Where do most GMP scope gaps come from?


Three sources account for most GMP scope gaps: reviewing documents one file at a time instead of cross-referencing disciplines, failing to update scope packages when addenda arrive, and writing vague scope language like "as per plans and specs" against an incomplete document set.
